summary: Summation No. 32 reports on Occupation non-military activities in Japan for May 1948, with most economic statistics running through March or April. Politically the month was dominated by the Ashida coalition's dispute over suspending war-bond interest, settled by a one-year deferral, and by Cabinet struggles over the 1948-49 budget and local finance. The report reprints MacArthur's message and other statements on the first anniversary of the Constitution, the Cabinet's Second Economic White Paper and the Economic Stabilization Board's five-year rehabilitation plan. It records party conventions, the Diet's investigation of political donations, the dissolution of the purge committees with 301,815 persons purged, and war crimes trial totals. Economic sections give detailed output, trade, price, finance and labor series, including postwar highs in steel, paper and textiles. The social sections cover health, nutrition, repatriation, education, religion and the press. Historians will find the primary-source texts and monthly statistical series especially useful.
highlights: Cabinet accepted the Tomabechi plan deferring war-bond interest payments for one year from June, dropping 460 million yen from the provisional budget.
MacArthur's message on the Constitution's first anniversary, 3 May, warned against despotism of the left or right and urged local autonomy.
Cabinet issued the Second Economic White Paper on 28 May; the Economic Stabilization Board published a five-year rehabilitation plan draft on 17 May.
Purge machinery dissolved 10 May; total persons purged announced as 301,815.
Maritime Safety Board activated 1 May; Impeachment Court established with Gisai Oniarau as first president.
April pig iron (55,072 tons) and steel ingots (118,557 tons) set new postwar records; paper reached a postwar high of 37,983 tons.
Ministry of Education policy of 7 May made Korean language and history optional in private Korean schools.
Of 33,635 Japanese repatriated 30 April to 27 May, 97 percent came from Soviet and Soviet-controlled areas.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover and front matter of Summation No. 32 for May 1948: table of contents for Parts I to IV (General, Political, Economic, Social, with 109 numbered charts), plus separate lists of charts, maps and graphs by subject, from industrial production indexes to repatriation, textbooks and film production, ending with Men of Japan.

sections.title: Part I: General
sections.summary: Digest of the month: no SCAP reorganization; political, economic and social paragraphs summarizing the detailed Parts.

sections.title: Section 1: Organization Under SCAP
sections.summary: A single paragraph states that the non-military organization of General Headquarters, SCAP, underwent no change during May 1948. It is the shortest section of the Part I summary, and the page introduces the Political Activities section that follows.

sections.title: Section 2: Political Activities
sections.summary: Summarizes May politics: the 3 May Constitution anniversary, the war-bond interest dispute ending in a one-year deferral compromise, Cabinet administrative reorganization, demobilization placed under the Welfare Ministry, and 16 laws enacted. Party conventions, dissolution of the purge committees with 301,815 purged, the Maritime Safety Board, the Impeachment Court and war crimes trial results (53 suspects, 44 convicted) are also noted.

sections.title: Section 3: Economic Activities
sections.summary: April production rose in coke (233,940 tons), pig iron, steel ingots, cement, paper and textiles, with silk and cotton fabric at postwar highs. Also covered: first-quarter trade deficit of $151.8 million, ration needs met from carryover stocks, calmer labor relations, tax receipts above estimate, antitrust rulings, machine-tool reparations shipments and eclipse observations.

sections.title: Section 4: Social Activities
sections.summary: Reports 3,237 communicable disease cases and 326 deaths in April, rising medical supply output, 123,511 orphans, and 33,635 repatriates, 97 percent from Soviet areas. Education covers the 7 May Korean school policy; religion notes the new National Christian Council; culture notes 379 Meiji historic sites delisted; media covers newspaper circulation, translation rights and broadcasts.

sections.title: Part II: Political
sections.summary: Detailed political section: government and politics, public safety, legal affairs and war crimes.

sections.title: Section 1: Government and Politics
sections.summary: First anniversary of the Constitution, war-bond interest deferral, Second Economic White Paper, five-year rehabilitation plan, budget wrangling, Diet, party conventions and the purge.

sections.title: Anniversary of Promulgation of the Constitution
sections.summary: Marks the 3 May anniversary of the Constitution. MacArthur's message urges vigilance, local autonomy, free enterprise, responsible press and labor. Prime Minister Ashida, Speaker Matsuoka, Councillors' President Matsudaira and the Chief Justice spoke at a Diet ceremony before the Emperor. Fourteen first-year reforms are listed, from popular sovereignty and police decentralization to land reform and purges.

sections.title: War Bond Interest Payment Issue
sections.summary: The three coalition parties split over suspending war-bond interest, with ¥460 million due in June. The council issued two opposing reports on 30 April. Chief Cabinet Secretary Tomabechi proposed a one-year deferral on 8 May; Social Democrats accepted it 12 May with conditions, the Cabinet adopted it 14 May and formally announced it 22 May, while financial circles organized opposition.

sections.title: National Government
sections.summary: On 22 May the Cabinet set ten principles for administrative readjustment, including shifting authority to local governments and paying allowances to discharged staff. A 24 May rally of local-government bodies demanded abolition of about 20 central agency branches and new local taxes. Remaining demobilization work passed to civilian ministries on 31 May, with about 500,000 servicemen still in Soviet areas.

sections.title: Second Economic "White Paper"
sections.summary: The Ashida cabinet's 28 May report, reviewing ten months since the July 1947 paper, finds living conditions still hard but prospects brighter: coal reached 29.32 million tons (97.7 percent of target), rice delivery quota was met, and note issue fell early in 1948. It surveys war losses, production, trade, inflation, public and industrial finance, wages, rations, labor and construction, and urges self-support.

sections.title: Foreword and Basic Conditions of Postwar Economy
sections.summary: The foreword says hard living conditions persist, but coal output, expected Allied aid and full rice delivery brighten the outlook. Three basic handicaps are set out: war losses of about 20 percent of prewar domestic assets (45.7 billion yen at surrender prices), trade far below the 2 billion dollar level needed, and rapid population growth.

sections.title: General Survey of Present Economic Conditions
sections.summary: Population reached 78.62 million (October 1947 census) through repatriation of 5.77 million. Industrial production averaged 43.1 percent of 1930-34 in fiscal 1947, up 21 percent, with coal at 29.32 million tons. Rice crop was 59.67 million koku; trade deficit totaled 520 million dollars; note issue rose 103 billion yen but fell in early 1948; transport remained the bottleneck.

sections.title: Coal Production Increase and Power Situation
sections.summary: Priority for coal mines in materials, funds, rice and housing, plus the Emergency Coal Production Increase Program, produced a record 2.95 million tons in December. Coal allocation rose 30 percent, industrial allocation 46 percent, though quality fell. Drought and typhoon damage caused power shortages; November measures and a new allocation system helped, with 30.5 billion kWh generated in 1947.

sections.title: Situation in Manufacturing Industry
sections.summary: Output rose in every category except food processing and crude oil, led by metals (71 percent) and chemicals (31 percent). Finished steel reached 569,727 tons and pig iron 411,462 tons, short of the 675,000-ton program because of power shortage and unrealized North China coking coal imports. Cement reached 1.28 million tons, against a 1.67 million target; Occupation Forces took about 20 percent of steel and 50 percent of cement.

sections.title: Production in Agriculture, Forestry and Aquatic Industries
sections.summary: Fertilizer for rice rose to 4.3 kan per tan, about 60 percent of demand. Rice (59.67 million koku) and wheat and barley stayed below 1930-34 levels; the autumn typhoon cost 2.5 million koku of rice. Land reclamation lags, timber and charcoal pile up for lack of transport, and fish output was 62 percent of the prewar average.

sections.title: Transportation and Communication
sections.summary: Government railways carried 112 million tons (85 percent of requirements), and a January 1948 cabinet decision gave rail priority similar to coal. Coastal shipping handled over 10.68 million tons, up 88 percent, though ports operate at 40 to 60 percent of prewar capacity. Trucks lack tires and fuel; Tokyo telephones fail in 54 of 100 calls.

sections.title: Foreign Trade Returns
sections.summary: In 1947 imports were 526 million dollars and exports 174 million, leaving a 352 million deficit made good by United States relief funds. Imports remained mainly food, fertilizer and petroleum, with 68.2 percent for hunger and disease prevention. Textiles supplied over half of exports; 80 percent of imported cotton went into export goods, and surplus stocks of cloth and yarn accumulated.

sections.title: Prospects for Foreign Trade
sections.summary: Trade shifted toward East Asia (66.8 percent of exports) while 88.3 percent of imports came from the United States. Barter deals were made with the Soviet Union and an American firm; civilian trade opened in September 1947. Prospects improve with a 60 million dollar cotton loan, but dollar shortage and unsettled exchange rates remain obstacles.

sections.title: Trend of Inflation
sections.summary: The report defines official, black-market and effective prices and tabulates Tokyo indexes. Black-market prices rose faster than official ones until June 1947; after the price revision official prices jumped while black-market and effective prices slowed. Black-market retail prices rose only 16 percent from November to February, against 68 percent a year earlier.

sections.title: Currency Situation
sections.summary: Bank of Japan note issue grew 103 billion yen in fiscal 1947, ending at 218.7 billion in March, with a 40 billion rise in December. January and February 1948 showed declines through tax collection and curbed public payments. Deposits (128.5 billion yen net) fell short of the 232.3 billion yen needed by treasury and industry.

sections.title: Balance of Government Finance
sections.summary: The General Account was near balance after a pay-tax campaign lifted collections to 124.9 billion yen by March. The report notes unequal burdens on wage earners, income-tax payers rising to 28.6 percent of the population, tobacco monopoly sales shortfalls, and expenditures dominated by postwar costs. Special Account borrowing reached 66.8 billion yen, mostly taken by the Bank of Japan.

sections.title: Recent Condition of Industrial Enterprise Finance and Savings Accounts
sections.summary: Industrial financing grew 167.5 billion yen in the year, 32 percent through the Reconstruction Finance Bank; coal took 53 percent of its general-industry advances. Bank loans largely followed the priority table. The RFB sold only 22 percent of its bonds publicly, the Bank of Japan absorbing 75 percent. Savings campaigns raised deposits, but time deposits were only 21 percent of the total.

sections.title: Recent Conditions of Enterprises
sections.summary: Enterprises suffer money shortage and deficits because power shortages cut operations, wages rose (January 1948 averaging 1.6 times July 1947), and allocation procedures remained inefficient. Labor productivity was only 28 to 33 percent of 1935-37, but the report argues overemployment is smaller than commonly claimed. It urges efficiency, less price subsidy, and support for small enterprises through a new Board.

sections.title: Wage and Living Cost
sections.summary: Average manufacturing wages rose from 964 yen in January 1947 to 3,224 yen in March 1948; government salaries were raised to 3,930 yen in January. Wage differentials narrowed between male and female and skilled and unskilled. Food took 67 percent of family spending; real wages stood near 30 percent of prewar, and household deficits averaged about 7 percent in 1947.

sections.title: Demand and Supply of Living Necessities
sections.summary: Staple rations were fulfilled since August 1947 after emergency imported-food releases, and the rice quota was fully delivered by mid-March. Fresh food rations rose to about 70 percent of purchases by February under December emergency measures. Clothing supply for 1948 is at most two pounds per capita; household fuel is about 35 percent of prewar.

sections.title: Labor Situation
sections.summary: The 1 October 1947 census gives 33.88 million gainfully employed and only 672,000 unemployed, a figure believed greatly underestimated, with agriculture absorbing much of the postwar increase. Additional rations went to about 6.15 million essential workers. Unions numbered 36,471 with 5,993,613 members at end of November 1947, and dispute statistics are tabulated.

sections.title: Construction Works
sections.summary: Public facilities lag: flood restoration cost far exceeded the 5 billion yen appropriated for fiscal 1947, and river control protecting 1.04 million chobu needs about 150 billion yen. Overcutting threatens forests, with 1.68 million chobu awaiting afforestation. Only 145 kilometers of road were repaired, and housing losses equal a third of urban floor area.

sections.title: "Japanese Economic Rehabilitation Plan"
sections.summary: The Economic Stabilization Board's first draft five-year plan, issued 17 May, aims to restore the 1930-34 living standard by 1952. Targets include mining and manufacturing at 130 percent of base, coal 44,000,000 tons, exports of $1,646 million, national income of 121 percent, and 2,000,000 houses. It conditions success on ending inflation and securing foreign aid.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: The report calls 1948 a crossroads for beginning real reconstruction, with the aim of a self-supporting economy that lessens the Allied burden. It stresses maximum production recovery, curbing inflation, efficiency in administration, enterprise and labor, a guaranteed minimum living standard, restricted luxuries and mobilized domestic capital. Constructive outside aid will come only if Japan uses its own resources fully.

sections.title: Local Government
sections.summary: A national conference of town and village heads opened in Tokyo 13 May, the first since the war, with Prime Minister Ashida pledging the Government would resign if it lost popular support. Its six resolutions sought 10 percent more food output, funds for the 6-3-3 school system and a Ministry of Construction. A 27 May compromise settled the local finance dispute at 199,700,000,000 yen.

sections.title: The Diet
sections.summary: Fourteen bills were introduced 25 April to 25 May, including the Political Contributions bill, the National Government Organization bill and the Juvenile Guidance bill. Sixteen laws were enacted, among them Daylight Savings Time and Minor Offense. Committee chairmanships went to Social Democrats, Democrats and People's Cooperatives, and Oishi and Takahashi won the 21 May Miyagi by-election.

sections.title: Budget Action
sections.summary: A June provisional budget of 25,800,000,000 yen passed 28 May while the Cabinet wrangled over the 1948-49 general budget. Disputes covered rail and postal rates (3.5 times), a 3,731 yen wage base, war bond interest deferral, local finance and school funds. The Cabinet approved a 399,300,000,000 yen budget 30 May.

sections.title: Civil Service Institute
sections.summary: On 14 May the Civil Service Institute graduated its first class from a 100-day course in scientific personnel administration, an outgrowth of the Civil Service Mission and the National Public Servants Law of October 1947. Of 354 graduates, 126 return to ministries and 226 join the National Personnel Commission. A second class runs 2 August to 1 October.

sections.title: Hoarded Goods and Illegal Transactions Investigation Committee
sections.summary: The Diet's Illegal Transactions Investigation Committee, in its 30 April interim report, urged laws curbing secret political funds after 16 sessions and 45 witnesses on the Tsuji case. Four perjury indictments followed 10 and 12 May. Construction firms' donations touched Deputy Prime Minister Nishio, the Showa Denko case continued, and Chairman Muto defended the committee's methods against Democratic criticism.

sections.title: Political Parties
sections.summary: Party conventions and maneuvers dominated May. Democrats held their national convention 4-5 May and accepted the war bond interest compromise. Social Democrats moved to unify the party and set a policy on the Labor-Farmer Liaison Council. Democratic Liberals attacked the Cabinet, with three small groups joining them 25 May. People's Cooperatives met 15 May and lost their Osaka branch. Ashida proposed barring Communists from office.

sections.title: The Purge
sections.summary: The Public Office Qualifications Committee and Appeal Board were dissolved 10 May under Cabinet Order No. 62. Of 717,415 persons screened since 1946, 201,815 remained purged after 129 reinstatements on 22 May. Statistical tables follow. A new advisory group (11 May) and the Attorney-General's Investigation Bureau, with eight regional offices, took over continuing checks and enforcement.

sections.title: Section 2: Public Safety
sections.summary: Hoarded goods recovered in April were worth 123,296,141 yen, up 36 percent, mostly metals. March saw 180,850 offenses and 101,402 arrests; Tokyo's rate was highest. Recruitment of 36,000 new police was completed. Prison population was 89,234. April rail accidents numbered 596, March fires 1,806 with 28 deaths, and the Maritime Safety Board was activated 1 May.

sections.title: Section 3: Legal Affairs and War Crimes
sections.summary: The Diet elected the first Impeachment Court president, and passed the Administrative Execution by Proxy Law (6 May); the Minor Offenses Law was enacted 30 April. Seventy-nine atrocity investigations closed, leaving 897. By 20 May 666 war criminals had been tried, 617 convicted including 95 sentenced to death; Okada was sentenced to hang. The IMTFE held no session.

sections.title: Part III: Economic
sections.summary: Detailed economic section covering thirteen subjects from agriculture to science and technology.

sections.title: Section 1: Agriculture and Fisheries
sections.summary: Tenant land sales were 104,014 cho in April, cumulative 531,334 cho; livestock-farm retention criteria were set for about 158 farms. Agricultural cooperatives approved by governors reached 11,774. Livestock slaughter fell in February; milk output was 10,185,000 liters in March; 280 goats arrived from the Brethren Service Committee. March marine production was 111,575 tons; Bonin whaling landed 243 whales.

sections.title: Section 2: Forestry and Mining
sections.summary: April log output fell to 63,490,300 cubic feet, while 1947 fiscal-year logs totaled 752,916,200 cubic feet, 18 percent over goal. Firewood, charcoal and gasumaki figures are given. April coal production was 2,572,400 tons, nine percent under quota; fiscal 1947 coal was revised to 29,335,500 tons. Lignite, crude oil (15,630 kiloliters), drilling and March mineral gains follow.

sections.title: Section 3: Heavy Industries
sections.summary: April coke reached 233,940 tons, a fifth consecutive postwar record, and pig iron (55,072 tons) and steel ingots set postwar highs, though labor disputes cut rolled steel. Nonferrous metals, rubber stocks, petroleum, cement (169,050 tons) and construction are covered, as are 10 tugs and 13 barges for the USSR, fertilizers, chemicals, rolling stock, machine tools and machinery.

sections.title: Section 4: Manufacturing
sections.summary: Covers March food processing (flour 103,664 tons), sake output of 747,060 hectoliters and tobacco recovery after a strike. April paper reached a postwar high of 37,963 tons. Glass, ceramics, electrical goods (hurt by labor trouble), trucks, rubber, leather, agricultural implements, toys, buttons, watches and sewing machines are covered, with record alarm clock and phonograph record output.

sections.title: Section 5: Textile Industries
sections.summary: April set postwar highs in spun silk yarn, rayon staple and filament, and cotton and silk fabrics; raw silk stayed above the 10,000-bale goal at 10,310 bales. Raw cotton stocks fell 29,250,000 pounds with a 100,000-bale minimum backlog. Wool, hard and bast fibers, knit goods, clothing, dyeing and finishing follow, including GARIOA cotton yarn for fish netting.

sections.title: Section 6: Transportation and Public Utilities
sections.summary: Registered commercial vehicles fell to 161,320 in April, with about 67 percent operable; deadlining was blamed on fuel, tire and repair shortages. Government railways carried 312,127,898 passengers and 9,787,700 metric tons of freight. Coastal steel-ship cargo rose six percent. Power generation reached 3,878,000,000 kWh, mostly hydroelectric, while gas available for distribution rose two percent to 64,363,146 cubic meters. Gas curbs on industry were extended to 1 August.

sections.title: Section 7: Communications
sections.summary: The Cabinet approved a bill on 22 May creating a Ministry of Communications and abolishing ten local bureaus. April brought 1,303,346 telephones, record toll calls in nine cities, expanded overseas radiotelephone and radiotelegraph service, and 6,535,531 radio households. Postal mail, savings and money-order volumes rose. Equipment output dipped amid strikes, with 438,836 ministry employees, a March profit of 355,966,254 yen, and research on voltage regulators and tubes.

sections.title: Section 8: Labor
sections.summary: Labor relations were calmer than at any time since mid-1947 despite wage talks in nearly every industry. Prime Minister Ashida opposed revising labor laws; May Day rallies drew 300,000 in Tokyo. The Diet unanimously backed rejoining the ILO, over NCIU objections. Unions numbered 30,199 with 6,390,227 members. Strikes, production-control trials and grievance-machinery disputes continued, alongside labor education, wage and compensation data, and employment measures including a coal-mine freeze.

sections.title: Section 9: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: March imports were valued at $40,160,265, with about 77 percent from the United States, followed by Cuba and the Philippines. Exports were $11,606,301, two thirds to Asia, led by the Netherlands East Indies. Foodstuffs were 47 percent of imports and textiles 21 percent; textiles made up 69 percent of exports, mostly cotton goods. First-quarter trade with the United States showed a deficit of $133,121,288.

sections.title: Section 10: Rationing and Price Control
sections.summary: Staple collections were negligible in May, the second month rations came from carryover stocks, causing local delays; 137,620 tons of imported food were authorized, including 97,620 tons of sugar. Vegetable and fish per-capita supplies, fats, oil, salt, spinning and railway-car prices were set. Incentive goods reached farmers and coal miners; rents, family expenditures and the consumer price index rose.

sections.title: Section 11: Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Japan notes stood at 223.5 billion yen on 31 May. A nationwide financial reorganization of 15 May wrote off worthless assets, with about 18 billion yen budgeted for bank losses. Reconstruction Finance Bank loans reached 64.3 billion yen; 67 control bodies were closed; April tax receipts passed budget estimates; national debt was 358.3 billion yen.

sections.title: Section 12: Property Control and Reparations
sections.summary: Looted property worth 278,781 yen was taken into custody and restitution of 737,044 yen effected. The SCAP custody account reached 368.4 million yen, with a new German External Property Commission account opened. Rehabilitation borrowing was cleared for restricted concerns, 80 control organizations were ordered liquidated, and 50 holding companies were released; 9,967 machine tools had been shipped to reparations claimants.

sections.title: Section 13: Science and Technology
sections.summary: Twenty-one observation groups studied the 9 May annular eclipse, mainly at Rebun Island, with Japanese-American and Chinese-Japanese cooperation. Japan Academy prizes went to Koga, Fujiwara, Kotani and Tomonaga. Polyvinyl alcohol fiber, bojuntan coke and sea-water caustic soda were reported, along with society meetings, 2,353 standards in effect, and 346 patents granted in April.

sections.title: Part IV: Social
sections.summary: Detailed social section: public health and welfare, and education, religion, cultural resources and media of expression.

sections.title: Section 1: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: April recorded 3,237 cases and 328 deaths from 11 communicable diseases, with no cholera. Medical and dental supply output reached about ¥1.68 billion, up sharply on March. LARA relief arrivals reached 4,625 metric tons; 123,511 orphans were counted. Unemployment insurance replaced allowances on 1 May. Births, deaths and nutrition surveys followed, and population reached 79,690,953; 33,635 persons were repatriated.

sections.title: Section 2: Education, Religion, Cultural Resources and Media of Expression
sections.summary: The Ministry of Education announced a Korean schools policy (7 May), allotted cement, and set secondary and university standards, correspondence education rules and 107 million authorized textbooks. The National Christian Council was organized 17 May, and 379 Meiji historic sites were declassified. Media coverage covered opinion surveys, a 22-newspaper circulation survey, a 98-book translation list, radio, films, theater and three new SCAP libraries.
